data.title: Global ex-US equities retain bullish outlook despite tighter policy
data.description:
Global ex-US equities retain a bullish backdrop despite rising valuation and monetary-policy risks, according to Callum Thomas, Head of Research and Founder of Topdown Charts, who said the latest Federal Reserve rate hike reinforces a shift toward tighter global policy.

Thomas said his assessment of global ex-US, or rest-of-world, equities remains bullish in absolute terms, while the relative case against U.S. stocks is also showing signs of improvement.

Technical indicators remain supportive, with equities in an uptrend and breadth remaining strong. However, policy conditions that have provided a tailwind are beginning to turn less supportive, while valuations, although still reasonable and significantly cheaper than in the U.S., have already risen substantially.

Thomas noted that the bullish case is less compelling than it was in 2024 and 2025, when valuations were lower and monetary policy was moving toward rate cuts. The Federal Reserve's latest 25-basis-point rate hike to 4% adds to what Thomas described as a broader global shift toward rate increases.

He also pointed to the relatively high valuation starting point for U.S. equities, which could leave them exposed if the policy and inflation backdrop becomes less favorable.

On relative performance, Thomas said global equities are still in the process of turning around a roughly 15-year period of U.S. outperformance. Emerging markets have driven much of the improvement so far, while developed markets outside the U.S. have also shown signs of strength.

However, he said the macro and fundamental catalysts needed for a sustained shift remain inconsistent, with relative earnings performance still favoring the U.S. and the dollar continuing to hold support after a brief decline from its peak. A sustained period of dollar weakness and stronger earnings growth outside the U.S. would provide additional confirmation, he said.

Earnings are meanwhile emerging as a key support for the global ex-US outlook, Thomas said. All three major segments of global equities are seeing upgrades to long-term earnings-growth expectations alongside improving forward EPS trends.

Emerging markets, particularly Korea and Taiwan, are an important driver, while developed markets outside the U.S. are also seeing earnings growth accelerate.

Thomas said the combination of improving earnings, tentative gains in relative price performance and still-cheaper valuations supports the bullish absolute outlook, although the significant valuation re-rating and global shift toward tighter monetary policy mean risks have become less favorable than in previous years.

data.title: Volkswagen recalls more than 208,000 US vehicles over steering defect
data.description:
Volkswagen (VWAGY) is recalling more than 208,000 vehicles in the US after a steering-rack mounting bolt was found to be vulnerable to corrosion and breakage, potentially resulting in a loss of steering control.

The recall covers 208,724 vehicles, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. The affected models include certain 2018 Tiguan SUVs, 2018 and 2019 Atlas vehicles, and 2019 through 2021 Audi Q3 models.

The right-side steering-rack mounting bolt can corrode over time and fracture, the US auto-safety regulator said. A failure could lead to a loss of steering control and increase the risk of a crash.

As part of the recall, dealers will replace the affected steering-rack mounting bolt at no cost to vehicle owners, according to NHTSA.

Shares were trading about 7% lower on Friday.

data.title: Inflation nation: Are record income gains already gone?
data.description:
Americans' income hit a new record in 2025, latest data from the Census Bureau showed, shedding light on households’ financial well-being before the Iran war exacerbated inflation.

U.S. real median household income was $87,460 in 2025, up 2.6% Y/Y after adjusting for inflation and the highest since 1967, when the Census Bureau began tracking this measure.

But the figure is only 2.5% higher than the previous peak set in 2019, when households had a median income of $85,320. By comparison, median household income increased 19% during the six years before the pandemic (2013-2019).

Income growth in 2025 was not evenly felt among the top and lowest earners. While the top 10% of households saw income growth of 1.7% to $261,300, the bottom 10% saw a slight decline to just over $20,000.

"The median income for the top earners is increasing, while income for the lowest earners is stagnant," Kristin Seefeldt, associate professor of social work and public policy at the University of Michigan, told CBS News. "The tax code has been revised to lower marginal tax rates for everybody, and we see the top earners benefiting from that."

Notably, the pay gap between women and men narrowed in 2025 after two consecutive years of expansion. 

Among full-time year-round workers, median earnings increased 3.2% for women but did not change significantly for men. And women earned nearly 84 cents on the dollar compared to men. 

Meanwhile, there were 34.5M people living in poverty in 2025, 4% lower than the prior year. The official poverty rate fell 0.5 percentage points to 10.2% in 2025.

Social Security continued to be the largest antipoverty program, moving 28.8M people out of poverty in 2025.

The Census data does not reflect cuts to Medicaid and SNAP (or food stamps) under President Trump’s "One Big, Beautiful Bill" (H.R. 1), which was signed into law last year.

"Many of the policies enacted through H.R.1 are on a long fuse, with just some of the massive cuts taking effect last year and many more on tap in the coming years," said Wendy Chun-Hoon, executive director, Center for Law and Social Policy. "This means that the numbers we see today will only get worse in the future."

There are also concerns over whether wage growth can keep up with the inflation we're seeing now.

American Action Forum President Douglas Holtz-Eakin pointed to data for production and non-supervisory workers. Their average hourly earnings grew 3.8% from Dec. 2024 to Dec. 2025, while the Consumer Price Index went up 2.7% over the same period. 

"If one extends the window to be from Dec. 2024 to Aug. 2026, average hourly earnings rose 6.1%, but the CPI rose 6.1% as well," he said. "Real wages have been flat over the past 20 months – negative thus far in 2026 – and affordability problems have moved to the forefront."

The affordability crisis is straining consumers, but they continue to spend at a resilient pace while focusing on value. Dollar General (DG) CEO Todd Vasos said even those earning over $100K are shopping like bargain hunters, positioning the retailer to capture a broader demographic.

Other retailers that stand to benefit from this shift include Target (TGT), Walmart (WMT), Costco (COST) and Dollar Tree (DLTR).

data.title: Antibody therapy developer Electra upsizes IPO seeking nearly $350M
data.description:
Electra Therapeutics (ETRA), a developer of antibody therapies for immune-mediated conditions and cancer, upsized its U.S. initial public offering ahead of its trading debut on Friday, expecting to raise nearly $350M in gross proceeds.

In a statement late Thursday, the California-based biotech priced the offering of approximately 23.3M shares at $15 each as part of a listing on The Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol ETRA.

Underwriters will have a 30-day option to buy up to an additional 3.5M shares at the IPO price, the company said.

Earlier this week, Electra (ETRA) set its IPO terms for an offering of about 21.7M shares, seeking roughly $296.6M in net proceeds, assuming an initial public offering price of $15.00 per share.

Along with its existing cash, marketable securities, and cash equivalents, the company expects to use net proceeds from the offering to advance its lead asset, ipsoprubart, and for other business activities, including working capital purposes.

The monoclonal antibody therapy is currently undergoing a global Phase 2/3 registrational trial for newly diagnosed patients with secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, which is expected to complete enrollments in H2 2027.

The IPO is expected to close on Monday with Jefferies, TD Cowen, Evercore ISI, and Cantor serving as joint book-running managers.

data.title: StubHub's 'robust' Q3 trends should drive AEBITDA beat—Citi Research
data.description:
Riding the tailwind from the 2026 World Cup, Citi Research expects StubHub (STUB) to continue to see "robust" app downloads in the third quarter and deliver adjusted EBITDA near the high end of its guidance.

Given the upbeat projection for Q3 and the 30% retracement in the stock from the second quarter results, Citi’s Jason Bazinet views StubHub (STUB) as a Buy, fueling a 4% gain in the stock on Friday.

Bazinet believes the recent weakness in StubHub’s (STUB) shares can be attributed to fears the company would miss FY26 adjusted EBITDA guidance after reporting Q2 below expectations, concerns of a potential MLB lockout, and multiple compression from terminal-year AI risk.

However, based on Q3 download results, StubHub (STUB) should beat adjusted EBITDA estimates and reach 1.4M app downloads.

For FY26, Bazinet estimates StubHub’s (STUB) adjusted EBITDA of $419M and GMS of $10.9B.

The upgrade comes with a 22% cut to Citi’s price target for StubHub to reflect a lowered valuation multiple (9x from 10x) and a $0.30 per share discount to reflect a potential MLB lockout.

data.title: Ten consumer staples stocks with the strongest dividend growth grades
data.description:
Consumer staples stocks are drawing attention from investors looking for relatively defensive businesses and consistent shareholder returns as markets navigate changing economic conditions.

Companies selling everyday products and essential goods tend to have more stable demand than cyclical industries, while established dividend programs can provide another source of returns when investors are balancing income with potential capital appreciation.

Dividend growth is particularly relevant in the consumer staples sector, where many companies have long histories of returning cash to shareholders.

A sustained record of increasing dividends can provide an indication of a company's approach to shareholder distributions across different economic environments, although the ability to continue raising payouts ultimately depends on earnings, cash flow and balance-sheet conditions.

Against this backdrop, the following screen ranks the top 10 consumer staples stocks by Dividend Growth Grade. The list includes companies spanning household and personal-care products, tobacco, food and confectionery, wholesale retail and convenience stores.

Colgate-Palmolive (CL), Costco Wholesale (COST), Altria Group (MO), Procter & Gamble (PG), Philip Morris International (PM), and WD-40 (WDFC) lead the screen with the highest possible A+ Dividend Growth Grade. Casey's General Stores (CASY), Church & Dwight (CHD), Hershey (HSY), and Kimberly-Clark (KMB) follow with A grades.

The Dividend Growth Grade is part of Seeking Alpha's broader dividend scoring system and evaluates the consistency and magnitude of a company's dividend increases. Grades range from A+ to F, with A+ representing the highest possible grade. Under Seeking Alpha's framework, a B- or higher grade is considered a Buy, while a D+ or lower grade is considered a Sell.

data.title: Stock market edges down as Treasury yields rebound
data.description:
The stock market slipped Friday as Treasury yields reversed Thursday's retreat, with the 10-year note climbing back to the key 5.0% mark.

The S&P 500 (SP500) -0.2%, the Dow (DJI) -0.4%, and the Nasdaq Composite (COMP:IND) was virtually flat.

The stock market rebounded Thursday after Wednesday's selloff, which followed the Federal Reserve's first rate hike since 2023.

Fed Governor Michelle Bowman and Kansas City Fed President Jeffrey Schmid are set to speak, potentially giving clues on the central bank's rate path.

Elsewhere on the economic calendar, industrial production growth stalled in August, falling short of expectations, while August leading indicators slipped and missed the consensus.

The 2-year Treasury yield (US2Y) rose six basis points to 4.74%, the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield (US10Y) increased six basis points to 5.0%, and the 30-year Treasury yield (US30Y) advanced three basis points to 5.32%.

data.title: Fed's Bowman proposes bank stress testing changes to increase transparency, reduce SCB volatility
data.description:
The Federal Reserve Board will consider final revisions to its stress testing framework in coming weeks, Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said Friday.

The changes are designed to "improve transparency and public accountability, strengthen the reliability and accuracy of the models, and reduce the volatility of the capital requirements flowing from the annual stress test results," she said in a speech at an event in London.

Furthermore, she expects the Fed board to finalize reforms to risk-based capital requirements for large and small banks as well as improvements to the global systematically important bank (G-SIB) surcharge.

"In totality, these reforms create a durable and lasting framework to produce capital requirements that are rational, robust, aligned with risk, and transparent," she said.

She also discussed the results of the central bank's analysis of Silicon Valley Bank's 2023 collapse. Fed staff supervising banks should have known about Silicon Valley Bank's vulnerabilities as early as March 2022, about a year before the bank failed. Another factor contributing to the supervisory inaction was a "long-standing culture of risk aversion," she said.

The Fed will consider two final rules for revising the annual bank stress tests. The first final rule would require publishing detailed information on the stress test models and on the scenario design process, a move to make the Fed more accountable to the public. The second final rule would reduce the volatility of the stress capital buffer requirement by averaging the results of a bank's two most recent annual stress tests. The changes will also move the effective date of the new SCB to the following Jan. 1 from Oct. 1.  "The change aligns compliance to calendar year and provides additional time to implement the resulting capital requirements," she said.

Bowman said she'll also recommend a third proposal that will revise the 2027 test models to allow for public feedback. "The proposal will seek public comment on a revised model for noninterest income, which is the fee and trading revenue that banks earn from activities including wealth management, investment banking, and market making," she said. "This model would better capture business diversity across firms and would replace the existing noninterest income model for the 2027 stress test."

The stress tests should serve as a valuable tool in supervising banks, she said. "In theory, stress tests should identify unique firm vulnerabilities to material financial and nonfinancial risks. They should also provide insight into stressful scenarios that would cause those risks to materialize." 

The tests should identify a firm's vulnerability and allow them to address them before material financial and nonfinancial risks emerge, she said.

"Our approach will achieve this increased transparency and public accountability while making capital-related stress testing more accurate, effective, predictable, and fair," Bowman said in her conclusion.
